title: Preemptive analgesia in dentoalveolar procedures
summary: This study examines how preemptive pain management can help reduce (1) pain during and (2) after surgery, as well as (3) the need for pain medication after the procedure. It compares whether taking ibuprofen or etoricoxib before surgery is more effective than not taking any preventive pain medication. The study involves patients aged 18 to 65 years who have undergone a dental or implant surgery at the Clinic for Oral and Maxillofacial Surgery, University Medical Center Mainz. The main focus is to measure the intensity of pain during and after the procedure using a 10-point pain scale. Additionally, the study looks at how long it takes for patients to need pain medication after surgery and how their oral health and quality of life develop over seven days. The goal is to evaluate the benefits of preemptive pain management in dental surgery, as this approach is still rarely used in Germany despite new recommendations (Stamer et al. 2021). The study aims to identify which pain medication—ibuprofen or etoricoxib—is more effective and to assess the overall advantages of preemptive pain management in outpatient dental care.
conditions: Other disorders of teeth and supporting structures

interventions.name:
Ibuprofen
In the study, patients are enrolled only after administering preemptive analgesia; the choice of medication is based on the preferences of the treating physician. Therefore, it is a non-interventional study.

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
Consent obtained
patients capable of providing informed consent
aged between 18 and 65 years
undergoing implant placement or tooth extraction under local anesthesia.
Exclusion criteria:
- **Analgesic intake within 24 hours prior to the procedure**  
- **Chronic or long-term analgesic use, or use of psychotropic medication**  
- **Conditions contraindicating the use of non-opioid analgesics**: These patients will not receive preemptive therapy (e.g., heart failure NYHA II–IV, coronary artery disease, peripheral arterial occlusive disease, cerebrovascular diseases, hypersensitivity to the active ingredient or tablet components, active peptic ulcer disease or gastrointestinal bleeding, history of bronchospasm, acute rhinitis, nasal mucosa swelling, angioedema, urticaria, or allergic symptoms following NSAID intake, severe hepatic impairment [caution required in mild to moderate hepatic impairment]).  

**Other conditions excluding preemptive administration of ibuprofen or etoricoxib**:  
- Renal insufficiency with an estimated creatinine clearance < 30 ml/min  
- Inflammatory bowel diseases  
- Uncontrolled hypertension  
- Unexplained hematologic disorders  
- Pregnancy  
- Chronic pain syndrome  
- Lactation  
- Lack of consent/decline to participate in the study  
- Incapacity to provide informed consent  
- Age < 18 years or > 65 years  
- Concurrent jawbone augmentation (e.g., guided bone regeneration)  
- Complex augmentations or sinus lift procedures  
- Placement of more than four implants  
- Simultaneous soft tissue graft harvesting (e.g., from the palate)  
- Simultaneous bone harvesting (e.g., using a bone scraper)  
- Concurrent tooth extraction (exception: immediate implantation)  
- Osteotomy of more than two teeth  
- Extraction of more than ten teeth
